title: In-Game Item Marketplace
summary: Design a marketplace where players list, buy, and trade virtual items safely and fairly.
statement: Design an in-game marketplace. Players list items for sale, browse and search listings, and buy with in-game or real currency. Transactions must be atomic, inventories consistent, and fraud and duplication prevented. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: List an item for sale with a price.

requirementQuestions.question: How many listings, searches, and purchases per second?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: Can an item ever be sold twice or duplicated?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Selects between strong and eventual models and shapes conflict handling.

requirementQuestions.question: Fixed-price listings, auctions, or direct trades?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: How are scams, bots, and real-money trading handled?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Adds validation, rate limiting, and fraud controls to the critical path.

requirementQuestions.question: How long are transaction records kept for disputes?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines the data model, retention, and storage choices.

requirementQuestions.question: Should the marketplace stay up when the game servers are down?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How large is the listings index and how often does it change?
What write rate do purchases generate on the inventory and wallet stores?
How much history is stored per day?

keyDecisions.question: How is a sale made safe?
considerations: A single transaction moves item and currency, or a saga with compensation across services.

keyDecisions.question: How are listings found?
considerations: Search index for filters (type, rarity, price).
Database as the source of truth.
Index lag versus accuracy of availability.

keyDecisions.question: How is item ownership tracked?
considerations: Items are unique records with an owner; transfers are logged.

keyDecisions.question: How are prices and fees handled?
considerations: Fees and taxes as a sink in the economy.

commonMistakes: Check-then-update purchases that allow double sale.
Trusting the search index as the source of truth.
No audit log of item movement.
followUps: How do you support auctions with bidding?
How do you roll back an exploit that duplicated items?
How do you manage inflation in the economy?
How do you support trading between friends with confirmation?
